families.s: HSE tunnelling and construction work-in-compressed-air guidance
families.t: notification, contractors, competent roles, compression, decompression, medical surveillance, treatment, records, fire and emergency systems
f: The Work in Compressed Air Regulations provide a framework for tunnelling and other construction work under elevated air pressure.
Relevant work requires notification, safe systems, competent defined roles and suitable plant and equipment.
Compression and decompression procedures must be controlled, including HSE approval where required.
The compressed-air contractor has key duties because it controls the compressed-air operation.
A contract medical adviser and statutory medical surveillance are required for relevant workers.
Health effects can include decompression sickness, barotrauma and dysbaric osteonecrosis.
Emergency, fire, treatment, welfare, information and training arrangements must be established.
Health and exposure records must be maintained as required.
families.g: Compressed-air work risk depends on pressure, exposure and decompression profile, medical fitness, fire and plant systems, atmosphere, emergency capability and procedural compliance.

families.s: HSE compressed-air plant and airgun safety guidance
families.t: overpressure, bodily injection, particles, receivers, controls, overheating, maintenance, training and aerosol generation
f: Compressed air can cause bodily injection, skin penetration, eye injury and particle impact.
Overpressurisation can result from blockages, control failure, overheating, overspeed or external fire.
Compressor plant, receivers, dryers, coolers, distribution lines and pneumatic equipment require suitable design and maintenance.
Work equipment must be suitable, safe, maintained, inspected and used by trained people.
Compressed airguns can aerosolise metalworking fluid into inhalable mist.
Alternative cleaning methods should be considered where airguns generate hazardous droplets, dust or noise.
Compressed air should not be used to clean dust from clothing or the body.
Inspection, pressure protection, isolation, hose security, guarding and training form part of safe operation.
families.g: Compressed-air-equipment risk depends on pressure, stored volume, nozzle, hose, contaminants, receiver and control condition, blockage, temperature, maintenance, task and operator behaviour.

families.s: HSE automotive-glazing repair and replacement guidance
families.t: cuts, safer tools, glass weight, access, chemicals, roadside conditions, dynamic assessment, training and lifting assistance
f: Automotive glazing repair and replacement may be performed away from fixed premises, making instruction and training essential.
Broken glass and cutting tools create serious laceration risks and safer alternatives to long knives should be used.
Large commercial-vehicle glazing can weigh around 100 kilograms and create substantial manual-handling risk.
Difficult access to windscreens can add awkward posture and work-at-height hazards.
Sealants and other products require hazardous-substance assessment and skin or inhalation controls.
Roadside work requires traffic, weather, lighting and public-interface controls.
Mobile technicians need competence to perform site-specific dynamic risk assessment.
Vacuum or mechanical handling equipment can reduce manual effort where selected, inspected and used correctly.
families.g: Glazing risk depends on pane size and condition, access, cutting method, suction equipment, posture, team handling, chemicals, traffic, weather and site-specific supervision.

families.s: HSE vacuum lifting-equipment planning and safeguarding guidance
families.t: load suitability, suction capacity, reserve, alarms, inspection, attachment, power failure, exclusion zones and operator competence
f: Vacuum lifting equipment is widely used for smooth loads including glass, metal plates, slabs and boards.
The load surface, porosity, shape, weight and centre of gravity must be compatible with the lifting device.
Suction capacity and the number and arrangement of pads must provide an adequate safety margin.
Loss of power or vacuum requires suitable reserve capacity, non-return protection, warning or controlled lowering.
Work equipment must be suitable, maintained, inspected and accompanied by appropriate protective measures.
Pads, hoses, seals, gauges, alarms and attachment points require checks and maintenance.
People should be kept out of the danger zone beneath or beside suspended loads.
Operators need instruction, training and a planned method for attachment, travel, release and foreseeable failure.
families.g: Vacuum-lifting risk depends on load surface and mass, pad condition, vacuum capacity, leakage, power supply, attachment geometry, travel path, environment, inspection and operator competence.
